title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 1
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A council reports that since it began charging for bulky waste collection, the number of collections booked has fallen by 40 per cent, and concludes that residents are disposing of less bulky waste.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. The charge is £25 for up to three items.
B. The booking system moved online at the same time.
C. Charity reuse organisations in the area report a sharp rise in collections of the same kinds of item.
D. Collections are made within ten working days.
E. Neighbouring councils charge more.
questions.explanation: The waste is being routed elsewhere rather than reduced — and in this case to a better destination, which the council's own measure cannot see.

questions.prompt: A retailer found that stores that switched to LED lighting recorded higher sales per square metre than stores that did not, and plans to convert every store to raise sales.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. The chain converted its newest and busiest stores first, and those stores had higher sales per square metre before conversion.
B. LED lighting uses less electricity.
C. Conversion takes two days per store.
D. Some converted stores are in shopping centres.
E. Lighting is one of several refurbishment options.
questions.explanation: Conversion was allocated by existing performance, so the sales difference precedes the lighting.

questions.prompt: A university department reports that students who attend its optional statistics workshop score higher in the final examination, and proposes to make the workshop compulsory.
questions.question: The proposal assumes which of the following?
options: A. The workshop can accommodate the whole cohort.
B. The examination will remain unchanged.
C. Workshops are taught by permanent staff.
D. Students who do not currently attend would benefit as much as those who choose to.
E. Attendance is recorded accurately.
questions.explanation: The observed gap may reflect who volunteers; compelling attendance transfers the workshop but not the disposition that produced the gap. A is a capacity question rather than a premise of the inference.

questions.prompt: A food manufacturer reduced the sugar in its breakfast cereal by 30 per cent and reports that sales were unaffected. It concludes that customers did not notice the change.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. The reduction was made over eighteen months in small steps.
B. The company ran a large advertising campaign during the same period.
C. Sugar content is printed on the packet.
D. Competing cereals contain more sugar.
E. Some customers buy the cereal weekly.
questions.explanation: Stable sales could mean the advertising offset a loss of customers who did notice, so the outcome is consistent with the opposite conclusion.

questions.prompt: Every workshop run by the Calder centre that admits under-sixteens requires two supervisors. No session with two supervisors has been cancelled at short notice this term. Some sessions at the centre have been cancelled at short notice this term.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Two supervisors prevent cancellations.
B. Most sessions admit under-sixteens.
C. Sessions for adults are cancelled more often.
D. The centre is short of supervisors.
E. Some sessions at the centre do not admit under-sixteens.
questions.explanation: Cancelled sessions lack two supervisors, and admitting under-sixteens requires them, so the cancelled sessions do not admit under-sixteens.

questions.prompt: A rail operator reports that its new ticketing app has reduced queueing at station machines, citing that machine transactions have fallen by a third.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the claim about queueing?
options: A. How many passengers have downloaded the app
B. Whether the app accepts all payment methods
C. Whether the operator removed a number of machines when the app launched
D. How long the app took to develop
E. Whether staff assist passengers at machines
questions.explanation: Fewer transactions across fewer machines can leave queues unchanged or longer, so transaction volume alone does not establish the claim.

questions.prompt: A charity's fundraising director notes that supporters who attend its annual dinner donate more over the following year than supporters who do not attend, and proposes to invite every supporter.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the proposal?
options: A. The dinner costs the charity money to stage.
B. Invitations are currently sent to supporters whose past giving places them in the top tier.
C. Some attendees bring guests.
D. The dinner is held in November.
E. Attendance has risen each year.
questions.explanation: The guest list is selected on prior giving, so the donation difference exists before anyone attends anything.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer claims its insulation reduces heating bills by 25 per cent, citing homes where it was installed.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the claim as it applies to a typical home?
options: A. Installation takes a full day.
B. The insulation carries a 20-year guarantee.
C. Heating bills vary with the weather.
D. The homes cited were uninsulated before installation, while most homes now have some insulation already.
E. Some homeowners install it themselves.
questions.explanation: The saving is measured from an unusually poor baseline, so it will not transfer to homes that already have some insulation.

questions.prompt: An airline argues that its punctuality has improved, citing that the proportion of flights arriving within 15 minutes of schedule rose from 71 to 84 per cent.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
options: A. The airline lengthened its scheduled flight times by an average of 12 minutes at the start of the period.
B. The airline added new destinations during the period.
C. Punctuality is measured at the arrival gate.
D. Competing airlines report similar improvements.
E. Some delays are caused by air traffic control.
questions.explanation: Moving the target converts unchanged performance into a better statistic; nothing about the operation need have changed.

questions.prompt: A regional government reports that firms receiving its innovation grants grew faster than firms that did not receive them, and concludes that the grants cause growth.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. Grant recipients employ more graduates.
B. The grants are funded from general taxation.
C. Recipients report that the money was useful.
D. Firms may apply more than once.
E. Applications were scored by independent assessors, and firms scoring just above and just below the funding threshold grew at similar rates before applying, but diverged afterwards.
questions.explanation: Comparing firms just either side of an arbitrary threshold approximates a randomised allocation among near-identical applicants.

questions.prompt: Supporters of a proposal to extend library opening hours argue that borrowing will rise. Opponents reply that borrowing has fallen every year for a decade regardless of opening hours.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the opponents' reply?
options: A. Some libraries have closed in the same period.
B. Library membership is free.
C. The decade-long fall is accounted for almost entirely by reference lending, which has moved online, while borrowing of fiction has risen at branches that extended their hours.
D. Opening hours vary between branches.
E. Borrowing is recorded electronically.
questions.explanation: It decomposes the trend the reply relies on, showing the aggregate fall conceals a rise in exactly the category the proposal would affect.

questions.passageText:
A company that splits its shares two for one leaves every holder with twice as many shares, each worth half as much. Nothing about the business changes, and the total value of a holding is identical the moment before and after. The practice is nonetheless common, and the explanations offered for it are a useful test of how seriously to take arguments about market behaviour.

The oldest explanation is liquidity: a lower price per share makes small purchases easier, particularly where shares trade in fixed lots. This once mattered a great deal and matters less now that fractional purchases are widely available, which predicts that splits should have become rarer — and they have.

A second explanation is signalling. A board that splits is implicitly saying it does not expect the price to fall back, since a split followed by a decline is embarrassing in a way that no other corporate action quite matches. On this view the split conveys management's private expectation rather than any change in value, and studies do find small positive price movements on the announcement.

The third explanation is the least flattering and the hardest to dismiss. A share priced at fifty is not cheaper than one priced at five hundred, since what matters is the price relative to what the company earns; but survey evidence suggests some investors treat the lower number as cheaper. If that is right, splits work by exploiting a confusion, and their persistence is evidence about investors rather than about companies.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the liquidity explanation for share splits predicts that splits should
options: A. become more common as markets grow
B. occur only in companies with high share prices
C. raise the total value of a holding
D. have become rarer as fractional purchases spread
E. be confined to companies with many small shareholders
questions.explanation: The passage notes the prediction and adds that splits have in fact become rarer, which is what makes the explanation testable.

questions.passageText:
Animals isolated on islands frequently evolve to sizes conspicuously different from their mainland relatives. Large mammals tend to become smaller — dwarf elephants and hippopotamuses are known from several Mediterranean islands — while small mammals and some birds tend to become larger. The pattern is regular enough to have been named, and general enough to invite explanations that are more confident than the evidence supports.

The usual account combines two pressures. Islands have limited food, which penalises large body size, and often lack the large predators that made size protective on the mainland, which removes the compensating advantage. Small animals, released from predation, can afford the slower reproduction that larger bodies imply and gain the metabolic advantages of size.

Both halves are plausible and neither is universal. The pattern is stronger for mammals than for reptiles, weaker on islands close to the mainland where populations are replenished, and confounded by the fact that the fossil record preserves striking cases better than unremarkable ones. Reviews applying consistent criteria across many islands find the trend real but weaker than the textbook version, and absent altogether in some groups.

What the case illustrates is a difficulty that recurs wherever a pattern is named before it is measured. A memorable label collects supporting instances and repels exceptions, and the work of establishing how general the pattern actually is has to be done afterwards, against the label's own gravitational pull.
questions.prompt: The usual account of the island size pattern combines limited food with
options: A. increased competition between species
B. higher rates of disease
C. greater seasonal variation in climate
D. the loss of migration routes
E. the absence of the large predators that made size protective
questions.explanation: Removing the compensating advantage of size is the second half of the standard explanation.

questions.passageText:
Where a school is oversubscribed and places are allocated by lottery, the resulting comparison is unusually informative. Applicants who win and lose the lottery are alike on everything that led them to apply, so differences in their later outcomes can be attributed to the school rather than to the families who chose it. Much of what is known about the effects of particular schools comes from this accident of administration.

The findings are more varied than either side of the argument usually reports. Some oversubscribed schools produce substantial gains for lottery winners; others produce none; and the schools that produce gains are not reliably the ones with the strongest raw results, since raw results largely reflect who enrols. The useful output is not a verdict on a sector but a method for telling which individual schools add something.

Two limits deserve more attention than they get. The comparison holds only among applicants, so it says nothing about what a school would do for children whose families did not apply — and the decision to apply is itself unevenly distributed. And a lottery estimates the effect of attending one school rather than the alternative that applicant would otherwise have attended, which differs from applicant to applicant, so the same school can show a large effect in a district with weak alternatives and none where the alternatives are good.

The measured quantity is therefore a comparison, not a property of the school, and reporting it as a school's quality drops the half of the sentence that gives it meaning.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, a lottery makes the comparison informative because winners and losers
options: A. are alike on everything that led them to apply
B. attend schools of similar quality
C. come from the same neighbourhoods
D. are selected by the school on the same criteria
E. have identical prior attainment scores
questions.explanation: That similarity is what allows later differences to be attributed to the school rather than to the families.

questions.passageText:
An alphabetical index is so ordinary a feature of a book that its absence is more noticeable than its presence. It is also an invention with a history, and one that depended on a prior invention: the stable page number, which requires that every copy of a book be identical.

In a manuscript culture no such stability exists. Two copies of the same text have different line breaks and different leaves, so a reference can only point to a division of the work itself — a book, a chapter, a canon — and finding aids of that period accordingly point to divisions rather than pages. The apparatus of chapter divisions and marginal letters used in medieval reference works is a solution to precisely this problem, and a more ingenious one than the page number that replaced it.

Printing made identical copies, and the index in its modern form followed. It changed how books could be used: a work with an index can be consulted rather than read, and the practice of extracting a fact without the surrounding argument begins here. Contemporaries noticed and complained, in terms that reappear in every subsequent argument about new reading technologies.

The index also embodies judgements that its form conceals. Someone decided what counts as a topic, which mentions are substantive and which incidental, and what to call a thing that the author called something else. A good index is a piece of interpretation presented as a list, and its neutrality is the most successful illusion in the apparatus of the book.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the modern index depended on the prior invention of
options: A. alphabetical ordering
B. the printing press advertisement
C. the stable page number, which requires identical copies
D. chapter divisions
E. the table of contents
questions.explanation: In manuscript culture, differing line breaks and leaves meant a reference could only point to a division of the work.
